content.thinking:
I have a solid picture of the proposition. I am now pulling the full Mercury News endorsement, the Sacramento Bee yes endorsement, the SF Chronicle, PPIC analysis, and the OC Register no endorsement.

I am examining Civil Code 2924.13 and its exemption for middle-class home ownership loans under this chapter. I also noted the 30% attorney fee cap on construction defect claims for qualified builder homes as a significant consumer protection reduction.

Builders can obtain releases after repairs and communicate directly with homeowners during prelitigation. The qualified builder option is voluntary, but buyers of those homes face weaker defect remedies. This tradeoff is disclosed.

Condo construction defect litigation has suppressed attached housing in California. Some reform could increase supply. The 30% contingency cap is modest because typical fees run 33 to 40 percent and courts can approve higher amounts. The larger changes are procedural: more detailed notice, releases after repairs, and dismissal if the claimant fails to proceed with prelitigation.

Qualified new homes are not public works, so prevailing wage does not apply automatically. The qualified builder option only includes labor protections through PRC 21080.66.

Regulations are exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act. This reduces public process for rulemaking.

Amendments require a 60 percent vote in each house. This makes future fixes harder than ordinary statutes.

The bond statement says this is not state debt. It is only agency debt. CalHFA is a state agency.

CalHFA revenue bonds are not general obligations, though political pressure for a bailout remains.

The program requires buyers to retain a licensed real estate agent. That requirement benefits major funders and looks like rent-seeking.

Down payments must come from sources other than grants or borrowed money. This is stricter than many programs. Family gifts may still qualify if they are not loans.

The core economic problem is monthly carrying cost and housing supply, not just the down payment. Adding a second mortgage increases monthly payments significantly. For an $800,000 home, the 17 percent rate adds roughly $905 per month at seven percent interest, or about $573 at the proposed three percent rate. Many households who cannot save a down payment also cannot afford that extra payment.

PPIC analysis shows fewer than forty percent of eligible renters could afford entry-level homes with these payments, and almost none could afford homes at the price cap.

The below-market rates are aspirational rather than guaranteed. The agency must set rates practical and favorable to applicants while covering bond payments. Subordinate mortgage investors without government guarantee will demand risk premiums. The three percent rate is speculative and unnamed in the legal text. Campaign claims of low interest are not binding caps.

Limiting the program to new homes does not fix the underlying supply constraint. It avoids bidding wars on existing housing but leaves construction costs, zoning barriers, and fees untouched. The 190,000-home estimate is a campaign-commissioned high-end projection.

The income ceiling is too broad. It includes households earning $200,000 to $400,000 per year. There is no first-time buyer requirement and no equity recapture. Existing CalHFA programs like MyHome and Dream for All use silent seconds that do not increase monthly payments and better target lower-income and first-generation buyers.

The initiative locks in an untested design. CalHFA or the Legislature could have done this without a ballot measure, and revenue bonds do not require voter approval. The 60 percent amendment threshold makes future course correction harder. Voters are asked to approve loan terms that do not yet exist.

Industry capture is evident. Supporters contributed $33.6 million while opposition spent nothing.

The major newspapers and most housing experts oppose the measure. The League of Women Voters, Mercury News, East Bay Times, OC Register, San Diego Union-Tribune, and Budget Center all reject it. CalMatters calls it uncertain and weird. The SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee, and McClatchy reportedly support it. Newsom also supports it. Broad labor and business backing does not outweigh the substantive critiques.

I am now weighing the arguments for voting yes. The program would impose no direct taxpayer cost if bonds sell and the loans work as designed. It would help households who can afford monthly payments but cannot save a lump-sum down payment, and reaching 20 percent equity could eliminate PMI. Restricting to new construction avoids pure demand-subsidy price effects. Broad eligibility also reduces red tape.

Organized opposition is thin. No official argument was submitted.

California's low homeownership rate is a structural problem. Homeownership builds wealth.

The qualified builder option includes labor protections for workers.

Real consumer safeguards are present: annual audits, fixed rates, no prepayment penalties, and fee caps.

If the program fails, the state is not legally liable. The measure offers option value.

The program would force buyers into a 97 percent loan-to-value structure. That is the same high-leverage 80/17/3 subprime pattern that amplified the foreclosure crisis. Second lien holders would be wiped out if home prices drop even slightly. This is a serious risk.

The 80/20 piggyback mortgage was a hallmark of the mid-2000s housing bubble. Borrowers avoided PMI by taking a second mortgage for the down payment. When prices fell, they had no equity cushion and defaulted. Those seconds were high-risk and many investors lost money. Prop 37 recreates that structure at massive scale ($25 billion), through a state agency, for new homes that may be in peripheral markets more vulnerable to price declines.

The program would be a risky experiment. High leverage combined with second mortgages in softer exurban markets, plus no taxpayer guarantee and political pressure, could cause foreclosures and credit damage for buyers and harm the state's reputation.

FHA loans already allow 3.5 percent down with mortgage insurance. Conventional loans allow 3 percent down with PMI. The 20 percent down payment framing is outdated. The real barriers are elsewhere.

The measure does not lower purchase prices. It replaces PMI with a second mortgage. PMI on a 97 percent loan is roughly $267 to $533 per month. The proposed second lien would cost about $900 per month for thirty years and never drops off. That lien must also be paid to sell or refinance.

A rough comparison shows the second mortgage would cost about $905 per month. That exceeds the PMI on a 97 percent first mortgage, which is roughly $500 to $970 monthly. The smaller first mortgage also carries less interest than the standard 97 percent loan. So the program would likely raise total monthly payments rather than lower them.

If the second mortgage rate is close to the first, total monthly payments could actually be lower than a 97 percent loan with PMI. The second lien also pays down principal, unlike PMI which is pure insurance. This suggests the program could work as a cheaper alternative if rates are reasonable.

Private market data shows piggyback loans typically cost one to three points more than first mortgages. The proposed program would be unseasoned and lack GSE backing, so investors will demand a higher rate than seven percent. At nine or ten percent interest the benefit over PMI disappears and the buyer is locked into a junior lien that is harder to refinance. Existing first-time buyer programs already offer silent seconds with zero to one percent deferred interest, making Prop 37 worse for qualifying households.

The program targets households that earn too much for existing first-time buyer programs. Many of these higher earners can already save a down payment or use conventional 3-5 percent loans. The campaign overstates how many people fit the "can afford the payment but cannot save twenty percent" category and understates that 3 percent down products already exist. The California Association of Realtors reports a median down payment of twenty percent, but this reflects repeat buyers with equity and family wealth rather than a lack of 3 percent options.

The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.

The California Homeowner Bill of Rights is a set of laws that provide protections to homeowners who are facing foreclosure.

- **Notification of foreclosure-prevention options:** Your servicer must try to contact you at least 30 days before starting the foreclosure process to discuss your financial situation and explore your options to avoid foreclosure.
Your servicer can then start the foreclosure process by recording a notice of default in the county where your home is located, and will then send you a copy within 10 business days.
Within 5 days of recording a notice of default, your servicer must generally give you information about options to avoid foreclosure that may be available.

Blog Post · October 7, 2026
How Many Might Actually Use the Down Payment Assistance in Proposition 37?
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
Eric McGhee (https://www.ppic.org/person/eric-mcghee/)
California’s homeownership rate is among the lowest in the nation—a full 10 percentage points below the average of all other states—and prices have spiraled beyond what many can afford. Yet for a large number of families, the down payment—not the monthly payment alone—is the wall they cannot climb. Proposition 37, a measure on the fall ballot, would offer a leg up to scale that wall. It would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to loan as much as 17% of a newly-built home’s purchase price for a down payment. Prop 37 is ambitious and could have a meaningful impact, but the challenges of California’s housing market and current interest rates will limit its reach.
The program has a high income ceiling: 200% of area median income, or in some locations up to $373,000 for a family of four in 2024, the most recent year with Census data. In that year, 91% of renters—the ones most likely to use the program—would have qualified. Qualification ran higher still among groups with the lowest ownership rates: 97% of renters without a high school degree, 93% of Black renters, and 95% of Latino renters.
The home price restriction is also generous. The sales price must fall below 125% of the county’s conforming loan limit—the ceiling on mortgages Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can purchase, which the Federal Housing Finance Agency sets each year and raises in high-cost counties. That would have covered a home sold for as much as $1.15 million in 2024. While still falling short in some markets, that number would also have beat the statewide median (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CAUCSFRCONDOSMSAMID) ($782,000 in December 2024) by roughly 50%.
But income eligibility is not purchasing power, and the math on buying has turned ugly. High prices are now paired with 7% interest rates (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/business/mortgage-rates-7-percent.html) that make a standard 30-year fixed loan with 20% down unaffordable for many. Capping monthly payments at 36% of monthly income (Fannie Mae’s maximum debt-to-income ratio), even an entry-level home at the lowest price range (defined here as the area’s 10 th percentile for new homes) would have been out of reach for 56% of California renters in 2024. Around the state, the median payment for such a home would have been $2,259, and as much as $4,195. One in four homeowners would have been unable to pay it.
Such costs erase much of Prop 37’s ability to address low homeownership rates among certain demographic groups. Among renters without a high school diploma, 71% could not have both qualified for Prop 37 and afforded an entry-level home in their area; three quarters of Black renters would have been in the same position. Latino renters were a partial exception: 39% cleared the bar, largely because they more often lived in lower-cost areas with incomes high enough to buy but still low enough for Prop 37.
Given these limitations, how many people could Prop 37 assist, and how would that compare to the number who might be ready for assistance? We don’t have data on wealth so we can’t say how many would be able to come up with money for a down payment. But setting that aside, if every loan went to a home at the maximum allowable price and drew the full 17% support, the program would have reached roughly 113,000 buyers in 2024—notable, though still far short of the more than one million units California is estimated to need (https://www.ppic.org/publication/housing-in-california/). If the state instead provided 5% of the maximum purchase price it would amount to 409,000 buyers. The full 17% applied to entry-level homes would be 560,000 buyers, and 5% support for entry-level would be 1.8 million. Buyers of cheaper homes will generally need more help, not less, so the 560,000 figure seems a reasonable central estimate that would provide full support for purchases at the low end of the market.
It is worth noting that subsidizing the highest-priced homes reaches farther as a share of potential buyers. The program’s $25 billion would be more than enough to cover the relatively small number of buyers qualifying at the maximum allowable sales price. Conversely, targeting lower prices expands the pool of potential buyers, but beyond what even $25 billion can reach.
Perhaps a better question is whether the program can help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. As of 2024, California needed to turn 1.35 million renters into homeowners to match the ownership rate in other states. The maximum 17% support for entry-level homes would have gotten the state about 41% of the way there. Maximum support for the maximum price would have barely made a dent (8%), while the lower five percent support for entry-level homes would have more than closed the gap (136%).
If Prop 37 passes, it will face additional barriers. Many renters would clearly fail to qualify for a conventional mortgage even with the down payment assistance, and many others might not be able to come up with any money for a down payment at all. Moreover, because the money must be spent on newly-built homes, the proposition’s success depends on builders expanding housing inventory.
At the same time, Prop 37’s $25 billion could meaningfully help California close its ownership gap with the rest of the country. The key will be to target, to the extent possible under the rules of the program, homes that are well below the maximum price allowed. Prop 37 might help Californians buy a home, but its dollars must spread across a larger number of lower-spending recipients to have the biggest effect.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
Research is complete. I will answer yes or no.

No. The measure does not reduce home prices or construction costs. It increases household debt by adding a second mortgage on top of the first. Subordinate mortgages without state or GSE guarantees will likely carry higher rates. The 3% bond rate is speculative.

Market-rate subordinate loans could cost more than existing 3% down products with PMI. The program is poorly targeted: it caps assistance at 200% AMI, lacks first-time buyer priority, and has no equity recapture. Even with help, most renters cannot afford entry-level homes.

The new-construction-only restriction does not guarantee more supply. It may inflate prices for eligible homes and steer buyers toward HOA, Mello-Roos, or wildfire-prone periphery areas. The campaign's 190,000-home estimate is a high-end commission figure; the LAO says the actual impact is unknown.

The measure also contains hidden consumer-protection giveaways. It modifies construction-defect procedures, caps attorney fees for qualified builders, exempts subordinate mortgages from Civil Code 2924.13 protections, mandates realtors, exempts rules from the APA, and requires a 60% vote to amend.

The $25 billion in state second mortgages would create bailout pressure during a downturn. High-LTV new-home buyers are the most exposed to being underwater.

This did not need to be a ballot initiative. Revenue bonds do not require voter approval, and locking an untested product into law is the wrong way to experiment.

The measure received heavy industry funding from realtors, builders, and carpenters. It had no funded opposition. Its framing that buyers need 20% down is misleading because 3-5% products already exist.

CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Zero Taxpayer Cost-No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
CON

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
State Revenue Bonds. Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects. Over time, investors are repaid with interest. The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds. The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
Some People Seek Down Payment Assistance. When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front-typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment. If people cannot afford the down payment, there are different government programs available to provide down payment assistance to eligible homebuyers. To cover the remaining cost of the home, homebuyers get a loan, called a mortgage. Homebuyers then pay off the mortgage by making monthly payments that include interest.
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). CalHFA is a state entity that administers programs designed to help low- and moderate-income Californians afford housing. CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.
Construction Defect Law. To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards. For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
PROPOSAL
Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program. Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price. (Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.) Homeowners’ monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program’s administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible. CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.
Buyers and Homes Must Meet Certain Requirements. To participate in a middleclass homeownership loan, people and homes would need to meet certain requirements. For example, an applicant would need to be a resident of the state and have a household income no more than double the typical income level in their area. For a home to be eligible for purchase through the program, among other requirements, the buyer would need to be the first purchaser of the home and the price could not exceed certain limits.
Housing Developer Options. Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program. Developers also could choose to participate in a “qualified builder option.” Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.
FISCAL EFFECTS
No Direct State or Local Costs. Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.
Other Potential Effects. A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37’s scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 37
VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 37: the California Middle- Class Homeownership & Family Home Construction Act. Proposition 37 creates affordable homeownership opportunities for working and middle-class Californians and encourages new home construction-with ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS.
California has the second-worst homeownership rate in the nation; rising costs push homeownership further out of reach every year.
With the statewide median home price now exceeding $930,000, a traditional 20% down payment can require saving over $186,000 just to get in the door. Teachers, nurses, veterans, and firefighters work hard and pay their bills. They can afford monthly mortgage payments but are locked out of homeownership in the communities where they live and work because down payment requirements are too high.
Proposition 37 gives working and middle-class Californians a fair shot at homeownership.
KEEPING HOMEOWNERSHIP WITHIN REACH.
Prop. 37 is a practical solution. It makes consumer-friendly, low-interest downpayment assistance loans available to qualified California residents for purchasing a newly built home, with no cost to taxpayers.
This is not a handout. Homebuyers must qualify for a mortgage, meet income requirements, pay at least 3% down, occupy the home as their primary residence, make monthly payments, and fully repay their loans.
Prop. 37 is designed for renters, first-time homebuyers, and working families who earn too much to qualify for renter assistance programs, but not enough to save the massive down payment required to buy a home.
“Proposition 37 will boost homeownership without burdening taxpayers. As a state revenue bond, downpayment assistance loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers, not taxpayers.” -Malia Cohen, California State Controller
BUILDS MORE HOMES, CREATES GOOD JOBS.
California hasn’t built enough homes to keep up with demand. By helping qualified buyers purchase newly built homes, Prop. 37 will help accelerate construction, creating thousands of good-paying jobs and generating economic investment.
Expanding the housing supply helps workers and families to stay in California, build equity, raise their children, and live in the communities where they work.
ZERO COST TO TAXPAYERS.
Taxpayer advocates and California’s Legislative Analyst agree: Proposition 37 has no cost to taxpayers. Loans are funded by private bond investors and repaid by home borrowers-not taxpayers.
STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND CONSUMER PROTECTIONS.
Prop. 37 includes fiscal accountability and transparency requirements, construction accountability standards, and annual audits detailing the status of loans made and the fund’s financial condition.
Consumer benefits include below-market, fixed-rate loans, protections from unfair lending practices, strict limits on lender fees, and no penalty for early repayment.
BROAD, BIPARTISAN SUPPORT
Proposition 37 is supported by Democrats & Republicans, labor and businesses, construction workers, taxpayer and housing advocates, veterans, the California Teachers Association, and United Nurses Association of California.
For generations, homeownership provided stability, security, and a path to the middle class. But today, that path is simply out of reach for too many Californians. Proposition 37 is a practical solution that tackles one of the biggest barriers to homeownership, without burdening taxpayers.
Vote YES to expand middle-class homeownership, build more homes, create good jobs, and give working Californians a fair chance to live, work, raise a family, and stay in California.
VoteYeson37.com
Danny Curtin , Director
California Conference of Carpenters
Fiona Ma , Boardmember
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA)
David West , Chair
California State Commanders Veterans Council

### Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025.
To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures.
On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.”
Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves.
Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements.
The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.

### What will the measure do?
The proposition creates a down payment loan program, totaling up to $25 billion, for middle-income families looking to buy a new home in California.
The program would be run by the California Housing Finance Agency, which already oversees several homeownership assistance programs.
The state would sell bonds to fund the program.
It would pay back investors using interest and loan payments from the program — not taxpayer money.
The California Housing Finance Agency would administer the program, including setting interest rates for the loans.
To qualify, prospective borrowers would need to buy a newly constructed home or a home that never has sold before, such as a commercial building that was converted into condos.
Borrowers wouldn’t need to be first-time homebuyers, but they would need to earn no more than 200% of the median local income; for a family of four in Los Angeles County, that amounts to no more than $216,200 a year.
There also would be limits on the sales prices of homes bought with help from this program.
While the exact price would depend on the county, generally the homes would need to sell for between $1 million and $1.5 million.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Buying a home in California requires a colossal amount of money — and coming up with a 20% cash down payment of $180,000 for a median price home is a staggering hurdle for many would-be buyers.
That down payment amount is based on the statewide median $900,000 price tag for a house, according to recent data from (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/sept2026sales) the California Assn. of Realtors. In Los Angeles County, the median price for a single-family home is $935,000. In Orange County, it’s $1.5 million.
Proposition 37 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-37-loans-middle-class-homeowners-voter-guide) on the Nov. 3 ballot would allow the state to amass a $25 billion down payment assistance program for middle-class households. For perspective on the enormity of the measure before voters, one of the state’s existing down payment programs, California Dream For All, launched several years ago with $500 million, just 2% of the funding involved in Proposition 37.

The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds.
The program would not be funded by taxpayers, but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages. The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov. Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José.
“Prop. 37 is a historic opportunity to expand homeownership opportunities for generations of working families — at zero cost or risk to taxpayers,” Newsom said in a statement.

But Proposition 37 carries a significant caveat: Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building, some critics said.
Also, the proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure is approved. And some have questioned whether there will be sufficiently robust interest from investors to buy the state-issued bonds that will be used to fund the down payment loans.
The concept of down payment assistance is not new. Cities and states, including California, have long offered such programs to low- and middle-income homeowners, either in the form of loans or grants, and there are reportedly more than 2,700 such programs (https://downpaymentresource.com/professional-resource/down-payment-assistance-continues-to-expand-in-q1-2026-reaching-2679-programs-nationwide/) across the country.
Nevada, Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York all have programs to help homebuyers afford a down payment. Since 2021, New York has dispersed $70 million (https://www.ncsha.org/hfa-news/new-york-state-homes-and-community-renewal-announces-major-milestones-in-expanding-access-to-affordable-homeownership/) in down payment assistance. In Massachusetts, more than $146 million has been doled out in down payment help to homebuyers since 2020.
How the program would work
Under Proposition 37, down payment loans would work like any other, and would carry an interest rate and payback period — all of which would be determined by the California Housing Finance Agency.
To qualify, borrowers would need to have lived in the state for at least a year and earn no more than 200% of the local median income; in Los Angeles County, for example, that equates to a family of four earning no more than $216,200 a year.

Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Loan Program
Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
Additional Titles
California Middle Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 37 is a citizen-initiated state statute submitted to the California Attorney General’s Office on August 15, 2025. To qualify for the 2026 ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On April 21, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that enough valid signatures had been verified for the initiative to qualify for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 37.
Proposition 37 would allow the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a new homebuyer assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Eligible buyers could receive a second mortgage covering up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, while providing at least a 3% down payment themselves. Eligibility would be limited based on residency, household income, home price, and other requirements. The measure would also give housing developers the option to follow higher labor standards in exchange for more flexible construction-defect rules.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 37 would have no direct costs to state or local governments because participating homebuyers would repay the bonds fully through their loan payments. The measure’s broader financial impact is uncertain and would depend on investor purchase of the bonds, the affordability of the loans compared with other programs, and whether the program increases home construction and homeownership.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports creating a state second-mortgage program to help eligible California homebuyers purchase a home, funded by up to $25 billion in bonds issued by the California Housing Finance Agency.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating the state second-mortgage homebuyer program.

### Pro:
Supporters say that Prop 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, not taxpayers.

### Con:
No official argument against Proposition 37 was submitted.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
##### Background
To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction.
Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards.
For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
##### Proposal
*Housing Developer Options.* Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program.
Developers also could choose to participate in a “qualified builder option.”
Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects.
In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.

Prop. 37 explained: Can a $25 billion bond make homeownership in California attainable?
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)
October 20, 2026 October 20, 2026
Republish

New homes under construction in Mountain House on May 28, 2022. Photo by Martin do Nascimento, CalMatters
In summary
A clever solution or a confusing gimmick? Like it or hate it, almost everyone has questions about Proposition 37. Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
It’s a bond, but not like any other bond on the ballot.
It promises to provide homebuyers with mortgages, but not your typical mortgages.
It would set up a down payment assistance program, but one unlike any other in the country.
There are plenty of consequential and controversial propositions (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/) on California’s ballot this year, but none as plainly weird as Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/).
Supporters call it an “elegant” solution to the fact that so many Californians can’t afford to buy a home. Detractors characterize it as a Rube Goldberg-esque gimmick (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/10/02/endorsements-props-2-37-wouldnt-yield-saner-state-budgets-more-housing/?clearUserState=true) that’s too clever by half. Virtually everyone, including some hired to analyze the proposition, has questions.
Here are a few of the big ones — with the best available answers.
Q: What would Proposition 37 do?
A: If it passes, the state would be able to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a new loan program to help people afford down payments on new home purchases.
$25 billion ? With a “B”? That’s a lot of money, even for a state with a $352 billion budget (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-gavin-newsom-final-budget-deal/) .
It is. But unlike other bonds on the ballot, this isn’t supposed to cost the state anything.
When the state sells bonds, it’s borrowing money. Most bonds, like Propositions 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) and 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/), would be paid back directly with tax dollars.
With Prop. 37, the state would act more like a loan broker. The California Housing Finance Agency would borrow the money from private lenders (by selling them bonds) and then re-lend that money to homebuyers. When the homebuyers repay those loans, the money would go back to the bond holders with interest.
Just the right amount of news

By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/).
Sign up for free
Δ
If homebuyers don’t make their payments, the private lenders would be left holding the bag, not state taxpayers. That’s according to the text of the measure, anyway, though some analysts (https://www.hoover.org/proposition-lab-proposition-37#:~:text=But%20a,period) have expressed doubt that state lawmakers could resist the political pressure to bail out homebuyers in the event of a wave of defaults.
Are these loans just home mortgages?
Second mortgages, specifically.
Buyers would still have to purchase a house the old fashioned way, by going to a bank or broker and taking out a mortgage that covers the bulk of the home price. But that still leaves a down payment. The median down payment in California is 20%, according to the California Association of Realtors — though it tends to be lower for first-time buyers. For an $800,000 home, that’s $160,000.
That’s a lot! Is this second mortgage meant to cover the entire down payment?
Almost all of it.
The program would allow these loans to cover as much as 17% of a home’s value, reducing the $160,000 to $24,000.
Is helping people take on more debt when they buy a home a good thing?
Homeownership is hopelessly out of reach for many Californians, even those who might otherwise be considered comfortably middle class. California has either the second-lowest (https://www.census.gov/housing/hvs/data/rates.html) or lowest (https://www.minneapolisfed.org/community-development-and-engagement/data-and-resources/homeowners-to-population-data) homeownership rate of any state, depending on how you measure it.
For many Californians stuck renting, high monthly mortgage payments — reliably higher (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/12/homeownership-vs-renting/) than a typical rent across much of the state — make homebuying a no-go. For anyone in that situation, tacking on a second mortgage with another monthly payment isn’t going to help.
But for some, it’s the size of the down payment that keeps homeownership out of reach. Roughly 40% of recent buyers turned to friends or family to help bridge this financial gap, according to a national survey (https://www.lendingtree.com/home/mortgage/down-payment-help-survey/#more-than-1-in-3-who-received-help-say-they-couldnt-have-bought-their-home-without-it). The gap is especially large in California, where home values are so high.
Asking a family to squirrel that much away is like asking them to “travel to the moon in a cardboard rocket ship,” Bob Hertzberg said in an interview.
Funny metaphor, but who is Bob Hertzberg?
He’s the former Speaker of the state Assembly, the former Senate majority leader, an active wheeler dealer in a wide variety of contemporary California (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-forever-solano-shipyard-deal/#:~:text=former%20Senate%20Majority%20Leader%20Bob%20Hertzberg) political (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-09-10/measure-ula-bill#:~:text=Bob%20Hertzberg) debates and Prop. 37’s singularly energetic author and hypeman.
Hertzberg has been working on this idea for years, along with the California Association of Realtors, and he says he’s come up with an admittedly unusual, but very “elegant” solution for middle-class renters unable to scrounge together a down payment.
If this passes, would I be able to get one of these loans?
If you’re a typical Californian, it’s quite likely you’d at least be eligible.
Under this program, anyone making less than double their county’s typical income qualifies, which ranges from roughly $116,000 in Imperial to just over $410,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. That covers roughly 90% of all renters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber), according to a recent Public Policy Institute of California analysis.
Hertzberg and other supporters think it’s a good thing that such a wide swath of California would qualify.
There are plenty of existing down payment assistance programs aimed at helping lower income (https://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/what-is-an-fha-loan/), first-generation (https://calmatters.org/california-divide/2024/01/dream-for-all-california/) or veteran (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) homebuyers, but Hertzberg argues that the broadly defined middle class needs help. Plus, the minimal qualifications will make it relatively light on red tape, he said.
But some opponents, like the League of Women Voters of California (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/), worry that offering a potential boost to so many would-be buyers will mean those who need help the least — people shy of the income cap, endowed with considerable wealth or able to borrow from family — will be the most likely to get the loans.
That, they warn, will only re-enforce the state’s existing economic and racial disparities (https://www.ppic.org/publication/wealth-in-california/).
What kind of house could a borrower get with one of these second mortgages?
Two conditions apply.
First, there’s a price cap. This gets a little technical, but basically the home has to be less than about $1 million in inland California and up to $1.5 million in Los Angeles, Orange County and the Bay Area.
Second, the home has to be newly built or newly converted into housing. In other words, the borrower has to be its first occupant. No re-sales.

Why only new homes?
This gets at a common critique (https://www.aei.org/research-products/report/determining-the-price-impact-of-harris-down-payment-assistance-proposal/) of down payment assistance programs.
Giving some buyers a financial leg up without changing the number of units in circulation just shifts around who gets a house and who doesn’t. It’s like reserving a seat for someone during a game of musical chairs. Your friend might get a spot, but the same number of people will end up on the floor when the music stops.
Worst-case scenario, the new injection of money just pushes prices up further.
Reserving these loans for new units, the idea goes, would help ensure that new supply matches the new demand, resulting in a net increase in the number of homes and California homeowners.
How many homes would actually get built thanks to this program?
It could result in the construction of as many as 190,000 homes, according to an analysis (https://voteyeson37.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Prop-37-Homeownership-Analysis-1.pdf) commissioned by the Yes on 37 campaign. But the author concedes that’s at the high-end.
To encourage the industry to build eligible homes, the measure includes a “qualified builder” option. If a builder agrees to abide by the measure’s price cap and accept legal responsibility if they violate some basic labor requirements, they’re shielded from construction defect lawsuits as long as they repair any future mistakes to a homeowner’s satisfaction. When disputes end up in court anyway, legal fees would be capped.
The actual number of new units depends on how many builders decide it’s worth it to get qualified, how many of these homes would have been built anyway, the price of home and how much of the down payment each borrower wants to cover with the loan, along with a whole bunch of other unknowns.
What other unknowns?
There are quite a few, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026) highlighted two big ones in its analysis of the measure.
We don’t know whether investors would actually buy these bonds, and if so, at what rate. We also don’t know how many buyers will actually want to apply for these loans.
Why might bond buyers not want to lend the money?
Financing second mortgages is considered riskier than funding the traditional kind, because the loans add to a borrower’s debt load, the first loan is first in line to be paid back and the second wouldn’t come with the implicit guarantee of either the state of California or federal mortgage giants Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. If the borrower goes bust, the investor is on the hook.
Typical investors would want to be compensated for all that added risk. That means high interest rates.
Right now, traditional mortgage rates are blowing past 7% (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/25/business/interest-rates-economy-markets-inflation-mortgages.html). Ordinary investors “are going to want a fair amount more than that” for an untested, riskier investment, said Edward Pinto, who co-directs the Housing Center at the American Enterprise Institute, a conservative-leaning think tank.
Is this why buyers might not want to make use of these loans?
It’s the main reason.
Even if the second mortgage came with a 7% rate, that could add an extra $1,000 to a new homeowner’s monthly debt payments, depending on the price of the home. That’s a steep price to pay for a lower down payment. Less than 40% of Prop. 37-eligible renters would be able to afford these higher monthly payments for an entry-level home, according to the PPIC analysis (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37?utm_source=ppic&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=blog_subscriber).
For a house priced at the top of the eligibility range, less than half of one percent of eligible renters would be able to afford it.
Is there anything the state could do to bring these interest rates down?
Public money isn’t supposed to subsidize or backstop these loans, so not directly.
But Hertzberg said he has a plan.
Philanthropic groups and do-gooder foundations — “the Giving Pledge people,” in his words — might be convinced to purchase the bonds at below-market rates, potentially as low as 3%. This would be in the civic-minded spirit similar to buying war bonds during the Second World War, said Hertzberg. But it might also satisfy certain corporate social impact requirements, non-profit mission statements and even federal community lending standards (https://www.federalreserve.gov/consumerscommunities/cra_about.htm).
He said he’s already spoken to some possible donors about this, but has declined to name names.
So what happens if either investors don’t buy the bonds, buyers don’t take out the loans, or both?
Potentially nothing.
At a recent panel discussion (https://players.brightcove.net/876630612001/2eCBwdutJ_default/index.html?videoId=6406972609112), Chris Hoene, executive director of the left-leaning California Budget & Policy Center, said he was skeptical that Prop. 37 would work as advertised. But he also said the downside is limited.
“It could still work, and if it doesn’t work, the state’s not really on the hook,” he said.
So he doesn’t really like it, but said it can’t hurt? That’s weird.
I told you.
For the record: This story was corrected to note that Prop. 37 loans could be used to purchase any home sold under the policy’s specified price cap, even if the builder is not part of the “qualified builder” program.

Will Prop. 37 Make Homeownership More Affordable? It’s Not Guaranteed
Understanding How Proposition 37 Could Affect Homeownership Affordability
August 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/), Nishi Nair (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/nishi-nair/), and Kristin Schumacher (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kristin-schumacher/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 37 on the November 2026 ballot would establish a “middle-class” homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. This assistance could only be used to purchase newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser. The program is intended to be self-sustaining because participating homebuyers — not the state — would ultimately repay the bonds through their mortgage payments.

Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
Supporting homeownership is an important strategy for promoting economic security and wealth building. However, it is unclear whether Prop. 37 would meaningfully help “middle class” Californians who face the greatest barriers to homeownership to afford a home.
As Prop. 37 would be financed through revenue bonds — which do not require voter approval — the program proposed by this initiative could have been enacted legislatively or a comparable program could have been established by the California Finance Housing Agency. Prop. 37 is a citizens’ initiative spearheaded by former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg.
What Would Prop. 37 Do?
The Middle Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0013A1%20%28%26quot%3BCalifornia%20Middle-Class%20Homeownership%20and%20Family%20Home%20Construction%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29_0.pdf) would direct the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to establish a middle-class homebuyer downpayment assistance program, funded with up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. The new program would:
Provide up to 17% of the purchase price toward the down payment , which could only be used to purchase new homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, where the buyer is the first purchaser.
Require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price toward the down payment. Combined with the 17% state downpayment assistance, this would reach 20% of the home’s purchase price and eliminates the need for private mortgage insurance. A conventional first mortgage would cover the remaining amount.
Require the downpayment assistance to be provided as a loan, not a grant, which recipients are likely to pay back monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage . This would be in addition to the homebuyer’s monthly payments on their conventional first mortgage.
Allow applicants to have incomes up to 200% of the Area Median Income (AMI) , which varies by region.
Cap the maximum home purchase price at roughly $1 million to $1.5 million, depending on the county and other factors. This is equivalent to a $170,000-$255,000 downpayment assistance cap per home.
Not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers , nor would recipients owe the state any equity gained in their home. These are requirements of comparable state downpayment assistance programs the state currently operates.
Allow home builders to become “qualified builders,” and have their developments automatically qualify for the program if they meet specified labor and enforcement standards.
How Would Income Eligibility for Prop. 37’s Downpayment Assistance Vary Across California Counties?
Prop. 37 would make a broad group of Californians eligible for downpayment assistance by allowing family incomes not exceeding 200% of Area Median Income (AMI) to qualify, a threshold that extends well beyond established downpayment assistance programs.
AMI represents the midpoint of family incomes in a specific area, adjusted for household size. In other words, half of households in an area have incomes that exceed 100% AMI and half have incomes below that level, so 200% AMI is roughly double what a typical family makes in the area. The limit is tied to local incomes, so whether a family income would qualify for Prop. 37’s downpayment assistance would vary significantly across California.
For example, a Budget Center analysis of Census Bureau data shows that a family of four earning up to $166,800 annually in Madera County or up to $375,800 annually in Santa Clara County could each qualify for assistance. However, the final dollar amounts would be set by CalHFA if Prop. 37 is approved by voters.
How Is Prop. 37 Different from California’s Existing Downpayment Assistance Programs?
California operates several (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/index.htm) statewide homeownership programs through CalHFA, but Prop. 37 would take a different approach that could hit family budgets harder, as participants are likely to pay back the downpayment assistance monthly as a fixed-rate second mortgage.
For example, CalHFA’s MyHome Assistance Program (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/homebuyer/programs/myhome.htm) and the Dream for All Shared Appreciation Loan (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/dream/) program both provide downpayment assistance through deferred “silent second (https://www.calhfa.ca.gov/myaccount/faqs.htm)” loans (also known as silent second mortgages). MyHome charges 1% simple interest on the assistance; Dream for All accrues no interest, but requires a 15% or 20% share of the home’s appreciation to go to the state. Under both programs, nothing is due on these silent second mortgages until the homeowner sells, refinances, or pays off the first mortgage. This ensures that the downpayment assistance doesn’t compete with the first mortgage, groceries, utility bills, or other basic needs in a family’s monthly budget.
Prop. 37’s approach is likely to require monthly payments. This is because CalHFA would issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, and by law those bonds must be repaid from the proceeds of the program itself — meaning the principal and interest of the second mortgages CalHFA issues. The second mortgages would need to generate steady, ongoing revenue to pay the debt from the revenue bonds. Language in the measure also states “a borrower may request a temporary hardship deferral of monthly interest payments on its middle-class homeownership loan,” further alluding to its intended structure.

Under Prop. 37, the second mortgage payment could also likely carry higher interest rates above conventional first mortgage rates. Although the measure states the intent to provide below-market downpayment assistance financing, it doesn’t guarantee it. The interest rate on the second mortgages would ultimately depend on the terms under which the bonds are issued and market conditions at the time of implementation, which are largely outside CalHFA’s control.
Revenue bonds that finance second mortgages are inherently riskier for investors because if a homeowner defaults, the first mortgage gets repaid before the second, leaving the bond investors more exposed to loss. Investors may therefore require a higher return to compensate for that additional risk, which could increase the interest rate on the second mortgage. This means Prop. 37’s second mortgage rate could land above the roughly 6.5% conventional first-mortgage rates buyers already face today. CalHFA wouldn’t set the actual rate or terms on the second mortgage until implementation, so the interest rate cannot be known before voters decide on Prop. 37.
Ultimately, while Prop. 37 could help get homebuyers to a 20% downpayment to avoid private mortgage insurance, the monthly repayment costs for the second mortgage could erode much of the benefit the downpayment assistance was meant to provide.
Would Prop. 37 Reach “Middle-Class” Californians Facing the Greatest Barriers to Homeownership?
Prop. 37 would make a broad range of households eligible for downpayment assistance, but income eligibility alone does not determine who can realistically purchase a home. Racial and ethnic disparities in income (https://www.ppic.org/publication/income-inequality-in-california/#:~:text=Overall%2C%20the%20highest,without%20college%20degrees.), wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/#:~:text=Wealth%20gaps%20by%20race%20and%20ethnicity%20are%20large.), credit access (https://www.epi.org/publication/chasing-the-dream-of-equity/#:~:text=Despite%20the%20bill%E2%80%99s%20intention%20to%20expand%20credit%20access%2C%20Black%20applicants%20are%20consistently%20more%20likely%20to%20be%20denied%20loans%20than%20applicants%20from%20other%20racial%20groups%20(), and housing affordability (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/HAI2025byEthnicity#:~:text=Meanwhile%2C%20only%2011%20percent%20of%20Black%20households%20and%2011%20percent%20of%20Hispanic/Latino%20households%20had%20the%20same%20ability.) mean that not all eligible families across California may be positioned to benefit from the program as proposed.
Prop. 37 would require the buyer to put down at least 3% of the purchase price, which would still be unattainable for many Californians. For example:
A house that costs $500,000 would require a 3% down payment of $15,000.
A house that costs $700,000 would require a 3% down payment of $21,000.
These upfront costs could be out of reach for many families, with the result that Prop. 37’s assistance could largely benefit families with incomes toward the higher end of the eligibility range. According to the Public Policy Institute of California, the median amount in Californians’ checking and savings accounts was just over $18,000 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/0525ttr-appendix.pdf) in 2025 dollars. This means that a 3% down payment could still almost or entirely clear out most or all of what an average family has in checkings and savings.
Prop. 37 could also reinforce economic, racial, and ethnic inequities in homeownership. The measure is intended to help “middle class” Californians, roughly defined as those with incomes between 80% to 200% AMI. White families are overrepresented among middle- and upper-middle-income Californians (46%), compared to their share of all California families (42%).
In contrast, Black and Latinx families are underrepresented in this “middle class” income range. This means that white families could disproportionately benefit from this program — even though white households already make up the largest share of homeowners (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) in the state, while Black and Latinx renter households face disproportionately high housing costs (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CHP_State-Housing-Needs-Report-2025.pdf).
Prop. 37 does not require applicants to be first-time or first-generation home buyers, further exacerbating equity concerns. Black and brown communities have been historically excluded from building wealth (https://apps.urban.org/features/wealth-inequality-charts/) and accumulating assets, making the barrier to entering the housing market even more pronounced. Families of color face occupational segregation (https://www.americanprogress.org/article/occupational-segregation-in-america/) that pushes them into lower-paying jobs. They are also less likely to inherit generational wealth (https://budgetmodel.wharton.upenn.edu/p/2021-12-17-inheritances-by-race/), and are more likely to be renters. (https://www.ppic.org/blog/californias-renters/#:~:text=Within%20the%20state,a%20college%20degree.) These factors make it substantially more difficult to save for a down payment, even at similar income levels. Additionally, data limitations often mask significant disparities in homeownership (https://www.urban.org/urban-wire/why-does-homeownership-vary-so-widely-within-aapi-community) access across racial and ethnic groups, especially among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander Californians.
Could Prop. 37 Encourage Sprawl and Harm the Environment?
By restricting downpayment assistance to newly built homes or newly created housing units converted from nonresidential buildings, Prop. 37 could push more “middle-class” housing onto land that’s not well suited for housing. Much of the land in California best suited for housing has already been developed (https://shou.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2025-02/recent-leg-actions-factsheet-updated-feb-2025_0.pdf), leaving remaining areas that are often far from job centers, prone to wildfire,environmentally sensitive, or important for agriculture.
While existing state down payment assistance programs are not immune to these concerns because they can also be used to purchase new homes, Prop. 37 goes further by limiting assistance exclusively to newly constructed homes. As a result, Prop. 37 could further direct “middle-class” housing demand toward suburban and exurban areas. This is a critical deviation from infill development — building on denser, already developed land — which has been the focus of state affordable housing and environmental efforts.
This pattern of building housing on the periphery of cities (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=IN%20THE%20LAST,a%20city%2C%20is) is known as urban sprawl (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf) and carries various environmental and equity considerations. Development in more suburban and inland areas can push Californians further from job centers, increasing their commute times and making it difficult to travel without a car (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2936977/#:~:text=People%20who%20live%20in%20large%20metropolitan%20areas%20often%20find%20it%20difficult%20to%20travel%20even%20short%20distances%20without%20using%20an%20automobile%2C%20because%20of%20the%20remoteness%20of%20residential%20areas%20and%20inadequate%20availability%20of%20mass%20transit%2C%20walkways%2C%20or%20bike%20paths). It may also encourage development in areas on the outskirts of cities that may cause new homes to infringe upon natural habitats and important agricultural lands (https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), especially in areas like the Central Valley. Sprawl can also lead to divestment from urban areas (http://urban.org/sites/default/files/2024-05/Patterns_of_Sprawl_in_Fresno_and_the_Central_San_Joaquin_Valley.pdf), which are often composed of communities of color, and concentrate investment in higher-income, suburban neighborhoods, further exacerbating racial and income inequality across the state.
What Other Homeownership Costs Could Come with Prop. 37’s New-Construction Requirement?
Prop. 37’s new construction requirement could steer homebuyers toward housing with higher out-of-pocket costs on top of their monthly mortgage payments. Unlike existing state down payment assistance programs, which can be used to purchase both new and existing homes, Prop. 37 would limit assistance to newly constructed homes. New construction homes are more likely to come with homeowners association (HOA) dues, Mello-Roos assessments, and home insurance challenges.
HOA fees are far more common in new homes as nearly 70% of newly built homes (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-housing-hoa-fees/) listed for sale nationally in 2024 were subject to HOA dues, compared with about 38% of existing homes. In California, more than a third of residents live in an HOA — including about 65% of all California homeowners. The average monthly fee is $280 (https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/09/condo-hoa-fees.html), and fees can rise up to 20% annually without a homeowner vote under current state law.
New construction in undeveloped areas of California also often comes with Mello-Roos (https://www.treasurer.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/2023_1.pdf) special tax assessments, which fund infrastructure like roads, schools, and utilities in newly developed areas and are layered on top of regular property taxes — typically adding another monthly fee to new-build homes for years.
California’s home insurance market also compounds the problem. Some state insurers have stopped providing coverage in many of the wildfire-prone areas (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CA%20lot%20of%20

It could reinforce racial and economic gaps: it gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers, could assist households earning more than $300,000 in some areas, and still requires at least 3 percent down.
Assistance is limited to new or converted homes with no requirement that they be near jobs, transit, schools, or services.
The Legislative Analyst says it is uncertain whether the program would result in more homes being built or purchased.

I will examine the legal text of the proposition. I need to review the construction defect provisions, moral hazard risks, and taxpayer bailout exposure. This will help me judge whether the policy is sound.

Prop 37 would issue up to $25 billion in bonds to fund second mortgages for new homes. Buyers would pay a 3% down payment. This directly addresses California's low homeownership rates and high down payment requirements.

The bonds would be repaid by borrowers, not taxpayers. The state and local government would face no direct cost.

However, the proposition does not guarantee below-market rates. Second mortgages are riskier than first mortgages and lack Fannie or Freddie backing. Investors will demand higher interest rates. The plan also relies on unnamed philanthropists buying bonds at 3 percent. If market rates apply, the second mortgage could add roughly $1,000 per month. That would wipe out the affordability benefit.

PPIC estimates that fewer than 40 percent of eligible renters could afford the higher monthly payments for entry-level homes. For top-tier homes, the figure drops below half a percent.

The plan would saddle buyers with more debt rather than lowering housing costs. Monthly payment affordability is the binding constraint for many potential buyers.

The income cap is set at 200 percent of median income. That equals roughly $300,000 to $400,000 in some counties. It excludes first-time and first-generation buyers. There is also no equity share recapture requirement.

The program would mainly benefit higher-income households already able to make a 3 percent down payment. This could widen racial wealth gaps, which explains the League of Women Voters opposition.

Limiting loans to new construction avoids bidding up existing stock. However, new homes are often expensive and located in sprawl areas with HOA fees, Mello-Roos taxes, and wildfire insurance issues. It also does not address core supply constraints like zoning, CEQA delays, or construction costs.

The program may not actually increase new construction if builders lack demand for the bonds.

A qualified builder option would also weaken consumer protections against construction defects. Builders who opt in face modified Right to Repair procedures and a 30 percent cap on homeowner attorney contingency fees. This is especially concerning because the program targets new home buyers.

Attorney fee caps on construction defect claims could suppress condo supply, since California has a history of such litigation. Steering buyers into those homes with weaker remedies is problematic.

There is also real taxpayer risk. Revenue bonds lack state guarantees, but political pressure to bail out bondholders or homeowners during a default wave could still arise.

The initiative would lock in an untested financial structure. CalHFA could have passed this through the legislature without voter approval, but the initiative prevents future fixes.

Voters are approving a blank check on loan terms. The state agency would set interest rates, repayment schedules, and underwriting standards after the vote.

The scale is enormous and the outcome is uncertain. It is unclear whether investors will buy the bonds or whether the program will actually reduce housing costs.

The $33 million campaign spending is entirely from supporters. No official opposition campaign exists.

Subsidizing demand without fixing supply constraints may raise builder profits and prices of eligible new homes rather than lowering them.
